title: Cloud, Containers & Serverless
requirement: Solid understanding of cloud deployment, containerization, CI/CD pipelines.

questions.question: How are containers different from virtual machines?
questions.answer: A VM is virtualized hardware with a full guest OS, gigabytes in size, minutes to start. A container shares the host kernel, is megabytes, and starts in seconds. The trade-off is weaker isolation, so multi-tenant workloads sometimes use VMs.
questions.keyTakeaway: VMs virtualize hardware with full isolation; containers share the kernel for speed and density.

rows.note: VM only; gigabytes, minutes to boot

questions.question: What problem does a container orchestrator like Kubernetes solve?
questions.answer: It turns machines into one scheduling surface: it runs the declared replicas, restarts crashed containers, reschedules pods when a node dies, and scales on load, with rolling updates and rollback. The cost is operational complexity, so small deployments often use managed platforms.
questions.keyTakeaway: Orchestration replaces hand-run deployments with declared replicas, self-healing, and rolling updates.

questions.question: How do Docker image layers work, and how do you keep images small?
questions.answer: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer, so I order from stable to volatile, dependencies before source, and a code edit keeps the dependency layer. For size I use a slim or distroless base and multi-stage builds that copy only runtime output.
questions.keyTakeaway: Layer order maximizes cache hits; multi-stage builds ship only runtime artifacts.

questions.question: What do you consider when running a rolling update in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: maxSurge sets how many extra pods are allowed during the update and maxUnavailable how many can be down. Customer-facing services typically use surge 1 and unavailable 0. Readiness probes send traffic to the new version only when it's serving. I define the rollback trigger before release.
questions.keyTakeaway: Tune surge and availability, gate traffic with readiness probes, and predefine the rollback trigger.

questions.question: When would you choose serverless functions over containers?
questions.answer: Serverless fits spiky, short, event-driven work: you pay per invocation and the provider handles scale. Containers fit long-running, latency-sensitive or stateful services, with no cold starts and predictable cost at steady traffic. So core services go in containers, and webhooks and scheduled jobs on functions.
questions.keyTakeaway: Functions for spiky glue; containers for steady, latency-critical, stateful services.

questions.question: Why do cloud architectures insist on stateless services, and where does state go?
questions.answer: A stateless service treats every request independently, so any instance can serve it, and scaling and rolling deploys get trivial. I move state out: sessions to Redis, files to object storage, durable data to a database or queue. I treat sticky sessions as debt.
questions.keyTakeaway: Keep compute stateless; push session, file, and durable state into purpose-built stores.

questions.question: How do you manage infrastructure across multiple environments without drift?
questions.answer: I define every environment in infrastructure as code, like Terraform, and provision only through it. Modules let environments differ by parameters only, and state stays remote and locked. We promote the same artifact and change only configuration.
questions.keyTakeaway: One parameterized module per environment, applied only through IaC with reviewed diffs.

questions.question: What are the real costs and limits of serverless at production scale?
questions.answer: Cold starts add latency when a new instance boots, hurting p99, and provisioned concurrency pre-warms at an always-on price. Time, memory and concurrency limits are platform ceilings, so I use shorter functions and queue buffering. Chatty fan-out can cost more than a container, so I track per-function cost.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pre-warm for latency, design inside platform limits, and watch per-function cost as traffic grows.

questions.question: When would you reach for a sidecar container versus an init container or a DaemonSet?
questions.answer: Sidecars run beside the main container for the pod's life and share localhost, like log shippers and mesh proxies. Init containers run to completion first, for things like migrations or dependency waits. A DaemonSet runs one agent per node, like log collectors. I pick by scope: pod-local, one-shot, or node-global.
questions.keyTakeaway: Sidecars share the pod's life, init containers run once before startup, and DaemonSets place one agent per node.

questions.question: How do resource requests and limits shape scheduling, throttling, and eviction in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Requests drive scheduler placement. Limits are the runtime ceiling: CPU overage is throttled, memory overage is OOM-killed. Guaranteed pods (requests equal limits) are evicted last, BestEffort first. I set requests from measured p95 usage. I always cap memory since it isn't compressible, and treat CPU limits skeptically.
questions.keyTakeaway: Requests drive scheduling and eviction protection; set memory limits always and treat CPU limits as optional.

code.snippet:
resources:
    requests:
        cpu: "250m"
        memory: "256Mi"
    limits:
        memory: "512Mi"

questions.question: When is KEDA the right choice over the plain Horizontal Pod Autoscaler?
questions.answer: HPA scales on CPU and memory, or custom metrics. KEDA takes its signal from an event source like SQS depth or Kafka lag, and can scale to zero. CPU is a lagging proxy for waiting messages, so queue workers belong on KEDA. I keep HPA for services whose load shows up as CPU.
questions.keyTakeaway: KEDA scales on external event signals and to zero; plain HPA only reads CPU, memory, or wired custom metrics.

questions.question: How do visibility timeouts work for queue-triggered workers, and what breaks when they are set wrong?
questions.answer: The queue hides a received message for the visibility timeout. The worker deletes it on success, otherwise it reappears, which is at-least-once. Too short causes duplicate work, too long leaves a dead worker's messages invisible. I set it above p99 processing time, heartbeat long jobs, and make handlers idempotent.
questions.keyTakeaway: A visibility timeout that expires mid-job re-delivers the message, so set it above p99 processing time and make handlers idempotent.

questions.question: How do you pair CDN caching with object storage lifecycle rules without breaking production?
questions.answer: A CDN in front of the bucket absorbs reads, and lifecycle rules move cold objects to cheaper tiers. The classic failure is deleting an object while the edge still considers it fresh, or code hot-linking the bucket, which gives NoSuchKey errors. I version the bucket, expire only noncurrent versions, and set explicit Cache-Control.
questions.keyTakeaway: Cache hot objects at the edge, tier cold objects with lifecycle rules, and align cache TTLs with object versioning so deletes never 404.

questions.question: Where should application secrets live: environment variables, a managed secrets store, or a vault sidecar?
questions.answer: Environment variables suit non-secret config. Secrets there leak through build logs, crash dumps and committed manifests. A managed store like Secrets Manager gives auditable, IAM-scoped access with rotation, and the app fetches at startup with its runtime identity. I never bake secrets into images, since every layer stays recoverable.
questions.keyTakeaway: Secrets belong in a managed store fetched by the runtime identity, never in env vars committed to manifests or baked into images.

questions.question: What does a sane container registry strategy look like, including image scanning?
questions.answer: One private registry like ECR inside the pipeline, with immutable tags. Production references a digest or git-SHA tag, never latest, and promotion rebuilds nothing: the digest that passed staging moves on. Every push is scanned with Trivy or similar, and I fail on critical findings in runtime dependencies.
questions.keyTakeaway: Tag images immutably with the git SHA, promote the digest unchanged, and gate deploys on critical scan findings.

code.snippet:
docker build -t "$REGISTRY/app:$GIT_SHA" .
trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL "$REGISTRY/app:$GIT_SHA"
docker push "$REGISTRY/app:$GIT_SHA"

questions.question: When is it worth putting a serverless function inside a VPC, and what does it cost?
questions.answer: Only when it must reach a database or cache in private subnets. Otherwise it's cost: traffic to public AWS services rides the NAT gateway, with hourly and per-gigabyte charges. Private endpoints for S3, DynamoDB and Secrets Manager avoid that, and are usually the first optimization. My default is functions outside the VPC.
questions.keyTakeaway: Put functions in a VPC only to reach private resources, and use private endpoints over NAT wherever the service supports them.

questions.question: How do you choose between RDS, Aurora Serverless, and DynamoDB for a new service?
questions.answer: I start from access patterns. For relational data with joins and steady load, it's plain RDS Postgres, the boring correct default. Aurora Serverless suits spiky or rarely used SQL workloads. DynamoDB wins when access patterns are few, fixed and key-shaped at large scale, but you design tables around queries upfront, with no joins.
questions.keyTakeaway: Default to relational Postgres, take Aurora Serverless for spiky SQL workloads, and pick DynamoDB only for fixed access patterns at large scale.

questions.question: What happens when a Lambda function exhausts its concurrency, and how do you contain the blast radius?
questions.answer: Concurrency is a shared regional budget, roughly a thousand by default. Exhaustion means 429 throttles: synchronous callers get errors and async invocations retry. I set reserved concurrency on critical functions so a noisy one can't starve the account, and put a queue in front of bursty producers so a throttle becomes queue depth.
questions.keyTakeaway: Concurrency exhaustion returns 429 throttles, so wall off critical functions with reserved concurrency and put queues in front of bursty producers.

questions.question: How do the cost models of managed Kubernetes, Fargate or Cloud Run, and Lambda actually compare?
questions.answer: Kubernetes on nodes is the cheapest raw compute, but the node pool bills whether pods use it or not, so it depends on bin-packing and operating time. Fargate and Cloud Run bill per running second at a premium, good for small teams. Lambda is nearly free when idle and most expensive at steady high load. I model all three against real traffic.
questions.keyTakeaway: Sustained high utilization is cheapest on packed nodes, sparse spiky load is cheapest serverless, and Fargate or Cloud Run buys the middle.

questions.question: How do you decide between active-passive and active-active for a multi-region architecture?
questions.answer: Active-passive keeps a second region warm with replicated data and health-check promotion. Recovery takes minutes, and one region writes, so consistency stays simple. Active-active gives near-zero failover but needs conflict resolution on stateful layers, and roughly doubles the bill. I decide by RTO, RPO and conflict tolerance, usually starting active-passive.
questions.keyTakeaway: Start active-passive for minutes-level failover at half the cost; go active-active only when latency or uptime contracts justify multi-master data conflicts.

questions.question: Beyond writing everything in Terraform, how do you detect and resolve infrastructure drift in production?
questions.answer: Drift is divergence between declared state and what runs, like console fixes during incidents. I run plan per stack in CI on a timer and alert on a nonempty diff. I never blindly reapply over a production change, since it may be a hotfix. I codify correct changes into modules or import them, and revert the rest.
questions.keyTakeaway: Detect drift with scheduled plans that alert on divergence, then codify or revert the change rather than blindly reapplying.

questions.question: How would you implement blue-green deployments for infrastructure using Terraform workspaces?
questions.answer: A core stack holds the shared stateful pieces: load balancer, databases, queues. Blue and green workspaces each bring up a full parallel compute stack. I apply the release to the idle color, smoke test, then switch traffic atomically at a listener rule. The old color stays warm for rollback through the soak period.
questions.keyTakeaway: Provision two parallel stacks in separate workspaces, shift traffic atomically at the load balancer, and destroy the old color only after soak.

code.snippet:
terraform workspace select blue
terraform apply -var-file="env/prod.tfvars"
terraform workspace select green
terraform apply -var-file="env/prod.tfvars"
# flip the listener after smoke tests, destroy blue after soak

questions.question: How do you make IAM least privilege practical instead of aspirational?
questions.answer: I generate it from evidence. Run the service in development with audit logging, then use IAM Access Analyzer or CloudTrail to produce a policy from the calls actually made. Every service gets its own role, with permissions boundaries. I prefer temporary STS credentials, and CI lints for wildcards.
questions.keyTakeaway: Generate policies from observed API usage, give each service its own role, and gate wildcards in CI rather than trusting review alone.

questions.question: How do you design retry and dead-letter behavior so poison messages cannot take down an event-driven system?
questions.answer: Every async consumer needs an explicit failure policy. Transient errors get retried with exponential backoff and jitter. Permanent ones like malformed payloads go straight to the dead-letter queue. Attempts are bounded, so a poison message can't block the queue head. I alarm on any DLQ depth, fix the handler, and replay through redrive.
questions.keyTakeaway: Retry transient failures with backoff, dead-letter after bounded attempts, alarm on DLQ depth, and replay after the fix.

questions.question: What must a service get right between receiving SIGTERM and the end of its grace period?
questions.answer: The grace period defaults to thirty seconds in Kubernetes. First stop new work: readiness fails and the pod leaves the endpoints, with a short preStop sleep for propagation. Then finish in-flight requests, return the queue message, flush buffers, and close database connections. Unfinished work dies at SIGKILL.
questions.keyTakeaway: On SIGTERM stop accepting new work, finish in-flight requests inside the grace period, and flush state before the hard kill.

questions.question: How do you keep cloud spend visible and controlled as the footprint grows?
questions.answer: It starts with allocation, because untagged spend is nobody's problem. I enforce tags like owner, service and environment in IaC modules, with a policy denying untagged resources. Per-team showback dashboards and budgets with anomaly detection page within a day. We clean up idle resources, and buy savings plans only for a provable baseline.
questions.keyTakeaway: Enforce tagging at provisioning, allocate spend to owning teams, and back alerts with scheduled cleanup of idle resources.
